newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany starts Nasdaq-style growth stock market.
newsitem.headline: Germany starts Nasdaq-style growth stock market.

text.p: Germany's new market for growth stocks started in a burst of publicity on Monday amid hopes that the system, modelled on New York's Nasdaq, will breathe new life into the country's cautious investment world.

Developed and promoted by the stock exchange, the so-called New Market is designed to encourage innovative young firms to tap into a small but growing demand in Germany for potentially high-yielding, risk-bearing investments.

But with only two companies having so far opted for the market, analysts are sceptical about the initiative, Frankfurt's latest bid to overcome a reputation for a lack of innovation and gain an edge over international rivals.
"Nowhere in the world can a German issuer raise equity capital under more attractive conditions than here in Germany," bourse board member Reto Francioni told a news conference.
He said he was sure that the New Market would outpace Nasdaq, the computerised inter-dealer system in the United States, which took 15 years to establish itself.
Aimed mainly at high-technology businesses, New Market offers firms advice and publicity on public offerings and a guarantee of liquidity after their stock starts trading.
In return, companies must meet strict entry requirements on issue conditions and transparency to reduce risks, including publishing quarterly results and using International Accounting Standards.
"If we want to access the right investors, we have to be able to do what British and American companies do," Francioni said.
But even Francioni had to admit that the German system was starting out small.

Just two companies -- bourse newcomer mobile phone service provider Mobilcom and engineering firm Bertrandt AG, which already trades on the regular market -- took part in the launch, far short of the 20 participants needed to form a growth stock index.
The stocks performed well on the first day, with shares in Mobilcom surging more than 50 percent from their issue price to 98 marks.
In the longer term, analysts believe there is a growing group of investors in Germany who are willing to accept higher risk for the chance of above-average returns.
"Think five, maybe 10 years from now and we should have a really vibrant growth stock market here," said Bank Julius Baer chief economist Gerhard Grebe.
"But this is not America. Studies still show that the average German company takes 50 years to go to the stock market. We will have a long teething phase," Grebe added.
The New Market will eventually be accessible elsewhere in Europe and the United States, once the German bourse moves to a fully electronic trading system at the end of 1998.

Germany is already working closely with the Euro.NM initiative, a group formed to promote links between France's well established growth stock market -- Nouveau Marche -- and emerging systems in Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany.

Over the next 12 to 18 months, Euro.NM plans to work on developing a common data feed and marketing plan for the four growth stock markets. Plans to develop a common trading platform were shelved because of technical problems.
Francioni said much work had yet to be done but the first and most difficult stage for Germany was over.
"We are not standing breathless at the starting block but reaching the finish with a smile after a tough run," he said.
"Times are changing fast," said Amsterdam Stock Exchange official Paul Arlman, in Frankfurt for the New Market start.

"The cultural change we see here in Germany is taking place all over Europe. Ten years ago your only goal in life may have been to run a family business. Now your only goal is to run a publicly listed company," he said.
